status: complete — selective in the travel narrative and the trials; see coverage_note; awaiting second-pass review
note: Indexed in sections along the book's own movement outward: the church in Jerusalem (1-7), Samaria, Saul, and Cornelius (8-12), Paul's journeys (13-20), and the arrest, trials, and voyage to Rome (21-28). Narrative throughout, so every entry carries a mode.
sectioning_note: As with Jeremiah, the status field names what is done.
prediction_note: The indexing order named Acts 2:44-47 and 4:32-37 'the strongest candidate for PR28, the Heavenly Palace.' Both are tagged, at high confidence, as exemplifies: a community converting property into provision for whoever lacks is the practice's positive form at the scale the practice names. A third positive anchor appears at 11:27-30, where the Gentile church at Antioch sends its surplus to Judea before the famine arrives. Before today PR28 had no anchor at all; it now has these three, a positive prophetic anchor at Isaiah 23:15-18, and three counter-examples.
coverage_note: Chapters 13-20 are indexed selectively, as a travel narrative: left out are the commissioning at Antioch and the encounter with Elymas (13:1-12), the synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch (13:13-41), Timothy's circumcision and the closed doors to Asia and Bithynia (16:1-10), Paul's break with the synagogue at Corinth and Gallio's tribunal (18:12-23), the disciples of John at Ephesus (19:1-7), Paul's plan for Jerusalem and Rome (19:21-22), and the journey through Macedonia and the night at Troas with Eutychus (20:1-16). Chapters 21-28, unindexed: the plot of the forty men and the transfer to Caesarea (23:12-35), Tertullus's accusation (24:1-9), Festus and the appeal to Caesar (25), and the opening and closing summaries of chapter 28 not covered by its entries.

entries.pericope: It isn't for you to know times or seasons… But you will receive power
entries.connection: The disciples' last question to the risen Christ is about timing — 'are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?' — and the answer declines it: 'It isn't for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority. But you will receive power… You will be witnesses… to the uttermost parts of the earth.' The Discipline of Unknowing is not indecision: one acts steadfastly while knowing one's understanding is partial. Here the not-knowing is commanded and the acting commissioned in the same breath, with C27's widest horizon. 'Why do you stand looking into the sky?'

entries.pericope: All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer
entries.connection: Between the ascension and Pentecost there is only waiting: 'All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.' C09's prayer kept by a community, and C13's ordinary faithfulness in the interval before anything happens. The replacement of Judas is made by prayer to the one 'who know[s] the hearts of all men' and by lot — a decision handed over rather than seized.

entries.pericope: We hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God
entries.connection: At Babel the one language was confused and the builders scattered (Genesis 11:1-9). At Pentecost the scattered languages are each spoken and each understood: 'Parthians, Medes, Elamites… Cretans and Arabians: we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!' Not one language restored but every language honoured. C27's circle drawn around every nation under heaven, with no one required to stop being who they are to stand inside it.

entries.pericope: When they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said… Brothers, what shall we do?
entries.connection: Peter tells a Jerusalem crowd that the man they crucified was raised and is Lord, and 'they were cut to the heart.' Their question is the beginning of every return — 'Brothers, what shall we do?' — and the answer is C19's door: 'Repent, and be baptized… for the forgiveness of sins.' The promise is extended to its widest: 'to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off' (C27). The same crowd that was told it had killed the Righteous One is the first to be offered mercy.

entries.pericope: They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need
entries.connection: The first portrait of the church is a shape of life: 'They continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer' — C13's ordinary faithfulness — and an economy. 'All who believed were together, and had all things in common. They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.' The Heavenly Palace asks a community in surplus to resist building monuments to its own comfort and to redirect toward the afflicted; this community converts property into provision for whoever lacks. The indexing order named it the strongest candidate for PR28, and on the definition it is: the practice at the scale the practice names, a community and not only a household. 'They took their food with gladness and singleness of heart' — C18's freedom from possession experienced as joy.

entries.pericope: Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, that I give you
entries.connection: Peter and John are on their way into the temple 'at the hour of prayer' when a man lame from birth asks them for alms. They stop — 'Peter, fastening his eyes on him… said, Look at us' — and give what they have rather than what was asked: 'Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, that I give you.' Spontaneous Service is pausing one's own work to help someone finish theirs and treating the interruption as the work; here the work interrupted is the hour of prayer itself, which is why the tag is medium rather than high. The fixed gaze before the gift is C16's attention to the one at the gate. The sentence is also the logic of Verbal Almsgiving — those without money give what they do have — though what Peter gives is healing rather than words, and PR21 is not tagged.

entries.pericope: Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?
entries.connection: The crowd stares at the apostles, and Peter's first move is to refuse the credit: 'why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?' C23's hidden life in public, deflecting the audience to its proper object. Then mercy to the guilty, framed as generously as the facts allow: 'Now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers… Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out' — C19's door, held open by one of the men they had made fatherless of his teacher.

entries.pericope: They recognized that they had been with Jesus… Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves
entries.connection: Before the council the rulers notice two things: the boldness, and the source of it. 'When they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.' C05's apprenticeship visible to its opponents — not credentials but company. Ordered to stop speaking, they answer with the Citizen-Stranger's limit: full respect for the court, and a loyalty above it — 'Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can't help telling the things which we saw and heard.' PR10's ultimate loyalty resting above any human decree, stated courteously to the decree-makers.

entries.pericope: Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness
entries.connection: Released, the apostles report to their own people, and the community's response to threats is to pray — Psalm 2 read over their situation — and to ask not for safety but for boldness: 'Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness.' C09's prayer as the place a threat is taken, and C17's public witness sustained by it.

entries.pericope: Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own
entries.connection: The second portrait, more exact than the first: 'The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own… neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds… and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need.' A named example follows — Joseph, called Barnabas, 'Son of Encouragement,' who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. The Heavenly Palace in its positive form, and the outcome Deuteronomy 15:4 promised — 'there shall be no poor with you' — recorded as fact. C18's detachment as the refusal to call anything one's own.

entries.pericope: While you kept it, didn't it remain your own?… You haven't lied to men, but to God
entries.connection: Ananias and Sapphira sell a property and bring part of the price as if it were all of it. Peter's words locate the sin precisely: not the keeping — 'While you kept it, didn't it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn't it in your power?' — but the pretence: 'How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven't lied to men, but to God.' They wanted the standing Barnabas had just received without the cost. The Hidden Life is the practice against exactly this reach for an audience, and the passage is its absence at its gravest: generosity performed for credit. C04's audit of consistency between private and public, and C12's proof falsified. The severity of the judgment is recorded in the text; the index anchors the diagnosis, not the death.

entries.pericope: If this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it
entries.connection: Imprisoned again, released, and brought before the council a second time: 'We must obey God rather than men.' Then a Pharisee's counsel that is itself a discernment test, C08's: 'if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it' — judge by what lasts, and wait. They are beaten and released, and depart 'rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus' name.' C17's cost of fidelity, received as honour.

entries.pericope: A complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service
entries.connection: The first conflict inside the church is about food for widows, and it runs along an ethnic line: Greek-speaking widows neglected in the daily distribution. The apostles do not defend themselves or the system; they convene everyone, propose a remedy, and the community chooses seven men — every one of whom has a Greek name, from the complaining side. The Architecture of Peace aims at repair rather than victory and concedes early and out loud; here the concession is the authority itself, handed to the aggrieved. The daily distribution to widows is Habitual Almsgiving made an institution, and the structure created to protect it is C16's service, with authority used for the most neglected.

entries.pericope: The Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands… uncircumcised in heart and ears
entries.connection: Stephen, accused of speaking against the temple, retells Israel's history as a history of rejected deliverers: Joseph sold by his brothers, Moses rebuffed when he tried to reconcile two Israelites — 'Sirs, you are brothers. Why do you wrong one another?' — and every prophet persecuted. 'The Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands.' The outward sign read inwardly, which is C06's; and the charge 'uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit' is Jeremiah 4:4 turned on its hearers. C08's true prophet and the pattern of his rejection.

entries.pericope: Lord, don't hold this sin against them!
entries.connection: The council rushes at him, drags him out, and stones him. Stephen, seeing heaven opened, kneels and makes two prayers that repeat Christ's from the cross: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!' and, with a loud voice, 'Lord, don't hold this sin against them!' Non-Retaliation in its final form — no return, not even in speech — and Shedding Harshness at the summit the curriculum names: prayer for the good of those killing him, at the moment of their violence. C03's hardest turn and C27's ocean. A young man named Saul is holding the coats.

entries.pericope: Those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word… There was great joy in that city
entries.connection: Persecution scatters the church, and the scattered become messengers. Philip goes to Samaria — to the people the Jews of Judea held at arm's length — 'and there was great joy in that city.' C27's circle widening through the very dispersal meant to end it, and C17's community at home wherever it is driven. 'Devout men buried Stephen, and lamented greatly over him.'

entries.pericope: You thought you could obtain the gift of God with money… for your heart isn't right before God
entries.connection: Simon, who had made himself 'some great one' by sorcery, believes, is baptized, and then offers money for the power to give the Spirit. Peter traces it to its root: 'your heart isn't right before God… ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.' C21's diagnosis from the act to the heart behind it, and C08's distinction between the true gift and power bought or performed. Simon asks for prayer, which the text leaves without an ending.

entries.pericope: Do you understand what you are reading? How can I, unless someone explains it to me?
entries.connection: Philip is sent to a desert road and finds a eunuch from Ethiopia — a foreigner, and a man the law excluded from the assembly — reading Isaiah 53 aloud in his chariot. Philip runs alongside and 'heard him reading,' and his first words are a question: 'Do you understand what you are reading?' He begins 'from this Scripture,' where the man already is. Listening as Mercy gives attention before concluding, and Philip hears the man before he speaks to him. Isaiah 56:3-5 promised the eunuch a name better than sons and daughters, and here it is given (C27). C06's opened understanding: 'How can I, unless someone explains it to me?' He goes on his way rejoicing.

entries.pericope: Brother Saul, the Lord… has sent me, that you may receive your sight
entries.connection: Saul, 'still breathing threats and slaughter,' is struck down on the road and blinded. The Lord sends Ananias, who objects with good reason: 'Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints… Here he has authority… to bind all who call on your name.' He goes anyway, lays hands on the man who came to arrest him, and his first words are 'Brother Saul.' Merciful Reintegration receives the repentant back without lingering shame or probation; Ananias has only God's word that Saul is 'praying,' and he receives him as family on that word. 'Something like scales fell from his eyes' — C06's opening of the eyes in its most literal form — and the door of C19 opened for the chief persecutor.

entries.pericope: They were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him
entries.connection: In Jerusalem the church will not have him: 'they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.' 'But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord.' One man stakes his own standing on a former persecutor and ends the probation the community would have imposed. Merciful Reintegration in its second act: not only God's acceptance but a brother's sponsorship, which is how a community actually lets a stumble stop being someone's identity. C16's authority used for the one nobody trusts; C13's community enlarged by it.

entries.pericope: Full of good works and acts of mercy… showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made
entries.connection: Tabitha of Joppa is introduced by her character before her name is finished: 'full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.' When she dies, the widows stand around Peter weeping, 'showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.' Mercy made with her hands, garment by garment, for women with no one to clothe them. Habitual Almsgiving as a rhythm of work rather than a sum of money, and the Sacrament of the Ordinary's claim that the road's highest expression is in its least glamorous settings: a needle, a coat, a widow. C13's ordinary faithfulness.

entries.pericope: So he called them in and lodged them
entries.connection: Cornelius, a Roman centurion, 'gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God' — Habitual Almsgiving in a Gentile soldier, and remembered before God. Peter, praying on a rooftop, is shown unclean animals and told three times, 'What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.' Then three Gentile men arrive at the gate asking for him. Peter has never eaten anything unclean, and he will say himself that 'it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation.' He goes down, and 'called them in and lodged them.' The Sacrifice of Routine is letting hospitality override one's own discipline when a guest arrives; here the discipline is a lifetime's purity practice and the guests are those it existed to keep out. The clearest anchor for PR20 in the index. At Cornelius's house Peter refuses worship — 'Stand up! I myself am also a man.'

entries.pericope: Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favoritism
entries.connection: 'Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.' A conviction Peter did not hold a week before, reached by sight — C06's perception corrected. The Spirit falls on the Gentiles while he is still speaking, and the Jewish believers with him are 'amazed.' Shedding Harshness is the widening of the circle of concern until no one stands outside it, and this is the moment the circle of the church itself is widened, by the man who had to be shown it three times. C27's ocean.

entries.pericope: You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!… But Peter began, and explained to them in order
entries.connection: Back in Jerusalem the charge is about the table: 'You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!' Peter does not defend his standing or attack his critics. He 'began, and explained to them in order' — the vision, the men at the gate, the Spirit falling — and ends with a question that puts himself under the same authority as his accusers: 'who was I, that I could withstand God?' The Architecture of Peace aims at repair rather than victory, and the dispute ends in agreement rather than defeat: 'they held their peace, and glorified God.' C27's circle confirmed by the whole community.

entries.pericope: When he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all
entries.connection: At Antioch the gospel crosses to Greeks, and Jerusalem sends Barnabas to look into it. He comes, sees 'the grace of God,' is glad, and encourages them to 'remain near to the Lord. For he was a good man.' Then he goes to Tarsus to find Saul, whom no one else would sponsor, and brings him to the work. C16's authority as an opener of doors for others, and C13's community where the disciples are 'first called Christians.'

entries.pericope: As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea
entries.connection: A famine is foretold, and the young Gentile church at Antioch responds before it arrives: 'As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea.' Surplus — 'as any had plenty' — redirected to the afflicted rather than kept against the coming scarcity, and proportioned to each one's means. The Heavenly Palace's positive form across a border, from Gentile believers to Jewish ones; and Habitual Almsgiving's measured share. C27's circle now running in both directions.

entries.pericope: Constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him… Peter was sleeping between two soldiers
entries.connection: James is killed and Peter imprisoned to be executed after the feast. Two pictures: the church — 'constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him' — and the prisoner, the night before his trial, 'sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains.' C09's prayer kept by a community, and C22's quiet soul asleep under sentence of death. When he knocks at the gate, the servant girl is so glad she forgets to open it, and the praying church tells her she is mad.

entries.pericope: The voice of a god, and not of a man!… because he didn't give God the glory
entries.connection: Herod in royal robes gives a speech, and the crowd shouts, 'The voice of a god, and not of a man!' He accepts it, 'and he was eaten by worms and died.' Set beside Peter two chapters earlier — 'Stand up! I myself am also a man' — the contrast is the narrator's: one refuses worship, one receives it. C22's humility and C23's refusal of the audience, shown by their absence.

entries.pericope: I have set you as a light for the Gentiles
entries.connection: At Pisidian Antioch the Gentiles ask to hear more, almost the whole city gathers, and opposition rises from jealousy. Paul and Barnabas turn outward with Isaiah 49:6 as their mandate — 'I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.' Expelled, they shake the dust from their feet and move on, and 'the disciples were filled with joy.' C27's widening, and C17's community that is driven out and keeps its joy.

entries.pericope: Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you
entries.connection: Healed a lame man at Lystra, the apostles are hailed as gods and a priest brings oxen to sacrifice. They tear their clothes and run into the crowd: 'Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you.' Worship refused at the moment it would cost them nothing to accept — C22's humility as accurate self-description. And a sermon to pagans from the ordinary world: God 'didn't leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.' C24's landscape as testimony.

entries.pericope: Through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God
entries.connection: Stoned and dragged out of Lystra as dead, Paul gets up, goes back into the city, and after Derbe returns to the very towns that had expelled him, 'confirming the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God.' C25's road that runs through hardship rather than around it. Elders are appointed in every assembly with prayer and fasting — C16's authority handed on.

entries.pericope: All the multitude kept silence, and they listened… to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things
entries.connection: The first great dispute of the church — must Gentile believers be circumcised? — is settled by a council, and the process is as instructive as the outcome. 'After there had been much discussion,' Peter speaks; then 'all the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul'; then James sums up. Listening as Mercy practised by an entire assembly before it concludes. The decision is aimed at peace rather than at victory for either party — 'we don't trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God' — with a few requests for the sake of table fellowship, and it is sent with men from both sides and a letter that 'rejoiced' its readers 'over the encouragement.' The Architecture of Peace at the scale of a whole church, and C27's circle written into its constitution.

entries.pericope: The contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark
entries.connection: Barnabas wants to take Mark, who had deserted them in Pamphylia; Paul refuses 'someone who had withdrawn from them… and didn't go with them to do the work.' The disagreement is sharp enough to separate them. Barnabas, true to his name, gives the one who failed a second chance without probation, which is Merciful Reintegration; Paul's refusal is recorded without comment. The index records the passage as it stands and notes, for a reader of the whole New Testament, that Paul later asks for Mark by name as 'useful to me for service' (2 Timothy 4:11). C15's conflict honestly left unresolved, and C16's question of who is fit to serve. Medium, because the text does not say Mark had repented.

entries.pericope: Whose heart the Lord opened to listen… come into my house, and stay
entries.connection: By a river outside Philippi, at a place of prayer, a businesswoman named Lydia 'heard us; whose heart the Lord opened to listen.' Hearing as the gift — C06's opened sight given to the ear. Baptized with her household, she presses hospitality on the strangers: 'If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.' C14's household opened as the church's first home in Europe.

entries.pericope: When her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone
entries.connection: A slave girl with a spirit of divination 'brought her masters much gain by fortune telling.' When she is freed of it, her owners do not rejoice; they see 'that the hope of their gain was gone,' drag the apostles to the magistrates, and have them beaten. A person valued only as revenue, which is C16's counter-portrait, and profit as the god that cannot bear a loss, which is C18's.

entries.pericope: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God… Don't harm yourself, for we are all here!
entries.connection: Beaten, their feet in stocks in the inner prison, Paul and Silas pray and sing at midnight, 'and the prisoners were listening to them.' C09's prayer kept in the dark, and C22's quiet soul audible through a wall. When the earthquake opens the doors and the jailer draws his sword to kill himself, Paul's first concern is the man responsible for their chains: 'Don't harm yourself, for we are all here!' The jailer washes their wounds and sets food before them; the man who locked them in becomes their host. C27's mercy reaching the warden.

entries.pericope: They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans… let them come themselves and bring us out
entries.connection: Offered a quiet release, Paul refuses to be hustled out: 'They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No… let them come themselves and bring us out!' Full participation in the civic order, including its protections, claimed on behalf of a community the magistrates had wronged — and then the departure they request. The Citizen-Stranger is not withdrawal from society; this is that posture using the society's own law.

entries.pericope: Examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so
entries.connection: The Bereans 'received the word with all readiness of the mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.' Eagerness and testing together, and the narrator calls it nobility. C08's test of every teacher, and the posture the whole curriculum asks of its own readers: 'This appendix exists so that you can check me.'

entries.pericope: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD… In him we live, and move, and have our being
entries.connection: Provoked by a city full of idols, Paul does not denounce it; he reasons daily in the marketplace and, before the council of philosophers, begins with their own altar: 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I announce to you.' Their acknowledgement of not-knowing becomes his starting point — the Discipline of Unknowing honoured in others before it is answered. 'He made from one blood every nation of men… that they should seek the Lord… though he is not far from each one of us. For in him we live, and move, and have our being' — C27's single human family. And he quotes their own poets: the Citizen-Stranger's full participation in the culture he addresses, without surrendering the claim that judges it. Medium on both practice tags; the passage is mission, not personal formation, and the tags anchor the posture it models.

entries.pericope: Because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers
entries.connection: In Corinth the apostle finds a couple of the same trade 'and lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.' The greatest missionary of the church supporting himself by stitching leather. The Sacrament of the Ordinary locates the road's highest expression in honest work in unglamorous settings; this is that, done alongside the preaching rather than instead of it. When he is afraid, the word is C22's: 'Don't be afraid, but speak and don't be silent; for I am with you.'

entries.pericope: When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately
entries.connection: Apollos is eloquent, 'mighty in the Scriptures,' fervent, accurate as far as he goes — and incomplete. Priscilla and Aquila hear him in the synagogue and do not correct him there. 'They took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.' Covering Weakness is the refusal to expose someone's mistake publicly when it would shame them, and this is its most exact enactment in the New Testament: the correction made in private, so that a gifted man can be completed rather than humiliated. The result is a better teacher — 'he greatly helped those who had believed.' C08's concern for accuracy, carried out with C15's care for the person.

entries.pericope: Many also of those who had believed came, confessing, and declaring their deeds
entries.connection: After the sons of Sceva are overpowered by a spirit that knows Jesus and Paul but not them, fear falls on Ephesus, and believers come 'confessing, and declaring their deeds' — naming plainly what they had done, which is the Failure Recovery Protocol's first step (medium: the passage is communal and occasioned by fear). Then the cost: 'Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.' C18's detachment, paid in full and in public.

entries.pericope: Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth… you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash
entries.connection: The riot at Ephesus begins with an honest sentence from a silversmith: 'Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth.' Religion defended because it is profitable — C18's counter-portrait — and a crowd that shouts for two hours, 'most of them didn't know why they had come together.' It is calmed not by the apostles but by a city official: 'you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash… the courts are open.' C15's de-escalation, practised by an outsider.

entries.pericope: These hands served my necessities… so laboring you ought to help the weak… It is more blessed to give than to receive
entries.connection: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders is the only speech in Acts addressed to believers, and it is an account of a way of life: 'serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears'; 'nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy' (C18); 'Take heed… to all the flock… to shepherd the assembly' and 'therefore watch' (C16's authority and C20's guard). Then the economic testimony: 'I coveted no one's silver, or gold, or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me. In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.' Work done with one's hands in order to give, which is Habitual Almsgiving built into the shape of labour, and the Sacrament of the Ordinary as its setting. They weep and fall on his neck.

entries.pericope: Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed… The Lord's will be done
entries.connection: At Tyre the whole church — 'with wives and children' — walks the travellers out of the city and kneels with them on the beach to pray. At Caesarea a prophet binds his own hands with Paul's belt to show what awaits him, and everyone begs him not to go. 'What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die.' 'When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, The Lord's will be done.' C18's open hand held by a whole household of faith, and C14's families present at the parting.

entries.pericope: Purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses for them
entries.connection: In Jerusalem the elders tell Paul that thousands of Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses. They ask him to join four men in a vow, pay their expenses, and be seen in the temple, 'that all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you.' He does it the next day. A concession made early and publicly for the sake of a divided community — the Architecture of Peace at personal cost, by a man who had written that he became 'to the Jews… as a Jew.' Medium: the gesture fails, and the riot follows from it.

entries.pericope: I persecuted this Way to the death… When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by
entries.connection: Seized in the temple, beaten, and carried up the barracks stairs, Paul asks to address the crowd, and in his defence he tells the worst thing about himself first: 'I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.' And to the Lord, of Stephen: 'I also was standing by, and consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him.' C04's audit spoken aloud before a hostile audience, without excuse, and C19's door named by the one who walked through it. The account of Ananias's 'Brother Saul' is repeated.

entries.pericope: God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!… I didn't know, brothers, that he was high priest
entries.connection: Struck on the mouth at the high priest's command, Paul retorts: 'God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!' Told whom he has insulted, he corrects himself at once and in public: 'I didn't know, brothers, that he was high priest. For it is written, You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.' The Failure Recovery Protocol asks for exactly this — the failure named plainly at the next available moment, without self-justification, and the same law that was broken quoted against oneself. The retort itself is Non-Retaliation's absence, recorded honestly in the apostle; the index anchors the recovery. 'The following night, the Lord stood by him, and said, Cheer up, Paul' — C22's quiet restored after the outburst.

entries.pericope: Herein I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men… I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation
entries.connection: Before the governor Felix, Paul describes his inner discipline in one sentence: 'Herein I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.' The verb is the athlete's — exercise, train — and the object is a conscience kept clear in both directions. The Moral Audit in its habitual form, practised rather than occasional. And the reason he was in Jerusalem at all: 'I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation' — the collection from the Gentile churches that 2 Corinthians 8-9 describes, delivered at the cost of his freedom. Habitual Almsgiving carried across the empire. C12's proof.

entries.pericope: When it is convenient for me, I will summon you… he also hoped that money would be given to him
entries.connection: Felix, who knows the Way well, sends for Paul and hears him reason 'about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come.' He is terrified — and postpones: 'Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.' The Failure Recovery Protocol says return the same day: not tomorrow, not after a suitable interval. This is the convenient interval, extended to two years, while he keeps sending for the prisoner in hope of a bribe and finally leaves him in chains 'desiring to gain favor with the Jews.' Conviction felt and deferred; C19's door seen and not entered, and C16's authority used for gain.

entries.pericope: I pray to God, that… all that hear me this day might become such as I am, except for these bonds
entries.connection: Before King Agrippa, Paul again names his past without softening — 'Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities' — and the voice that stopped him: 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads.' His commission is C06's: 'to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light,' and his preaching is C12's: 'doing works worthy of repentance.' Called mad by the governor, he answers courteously. And when the king deflects — 'With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?' — Paul's reply is a prayer for the good of every judge in the room: 'I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me this day, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.' He wishes them his freedom and spares them his chains. Shedding Harshness at its most courteous, toward those who hold him captive (medium: the prayer is evangelistic, and the practice is broader).

entries.pericope: I beg you to take some food… he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and he broke it… Then they all cheered up
entries.connection: Fourteen days in a storm, no sun or stars, 'all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.' A prisoner with nothing — no rank, no money, his advice already ignored once — stands up among two hundred seventy-six despairing men and speaks: 'Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you.' At dawn he begs them to eat, 'and when he had said this, and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and he broke it, and began to eat. Then they all cheered up.' Verbal Almsgiving is the alms of those without material means: seeking out the discouraged and giving them a good word as a genuine act of charity. This is that alms given by the poorest man on the ship to the whole ship. C22's quiet in a storm, and C28's ordinary act — bread, thanks, eating — as the turning point of the night.

entries.pericope: The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire, and received us all
entries.connection: Shipwrecked on an island, two hundred seventy-six strangers, prisoners among them, are met by people who owe them nothing: 'The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire, and received us all, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.' C27's mercy practised by outsiders to outsiders, and C16's care for the stranger in its simplest form — a fire in the rain.

entries.pericope: No doubt this man is a murderer, whom… Justice has not allowed to live
entries.connection: A viper fastens on Paul's hand, and the islanders read it at once: 'No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.' When nothing happens, they swing to the opposite error and call him a god. The same misdiagnosis Job's friends made, in a single verse: suffering read as proof of guilt in someone else. Interior Diagnosis traces failure to its root in oneself; this is the outward, instant version of the error it guards against. C03's judgment of the neighbour.

entries.pericope: When Paul saw them, he thanked God, and took courage
entries.connection: The chief man of the island 'received us, and courteously entertained us for three days'; Paul heals his father, and the island sends them on with what they need. In Italy, believers walk out forty miles to meet the prisoner on the road, and 'when Paul saw them, he thanked God, and took courage.' The encourager encouraged. C14's hospitality and C13's community, met on the road.

entries.pericope: Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house, and received all who were coming to him
entries.connection: In Rome, Paul quotes Isaiah 6 to those who will not hear — 'this people's heart has grown callous… Their eyes they have closed' — C07's blindness as the obstacle. The book then ends quietly, without a verdict: 'Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house, and received all who were coming to him, preaching the Kingdom of God… with all boldness, without hindrance.' A prisoner under guard keeping an open door. C17's witness inside the capital, and C14's house as its place.
